a OurBigBook.com
The Chinese remainder theorem says that if the positive integers m1​,…,mr​ are pairwise coprime and M=∏i​mi​, then for arbitrary residue classes ai​(modmi​) there is a unique residue class x(modM) satisfying
x≡ai​(modmi​)(1≤i≤r).
(1)
Equivalently, reduction is a ring isomorphism
Z/MZ⟶∏i=1r​Z/mi​Z.
(2)
For existence, put Mi​=M/mi​. Pairwise coprimality gives gcd(Mi​,mi​)=1, so Bézout's identity supplies an integer ui​ with ui​Mi​≡1(modmi​). Then
x=∑i=1r​ai​ui​Mi​
(3)
has the required residues, because every term except the ith is divisible by mi​. If x and y are two solutions, each mi​ divides x−y. Pairwise coprimality then implies that their product M divides x−y, proving uniqueness modulo M.

An odd composite number N with gcd(b,N)=1 is a Fermat pseudoprime to base b when
bN−1≡1(modN).
(4)
For N=35, the Chinese remainder theorem for unit groups reduces this condition to congruences modulo 5 and 7. Modulo 5, Fermat's little theorem gives
b34=b2(mod5),
(5)
so b34≡1(mod5) exactly when b≡±1(mod5). Modulo 7, the unit group has order 6, so
b34=b4(mod7).
(6)
The equation b4=1 in the cyclic group (Z/7Z)× has gcd(4,6)=2 solutions, namely b≡±1(mod7).
Combining the two independent sign choices by the Chinese remainder theorem gives
b(mod5)11−1−1​b(mod7)1−11−1​b(mod35)162934​​
(7)
and hence
35 is a Fermat pseudoprime to base b⟺b≡1,6,29,34(mod35)​.
(8)

The Chebyshev polynomial identity Tm​(cosθ)=cos(mθ) implies ∣Tm​(x)∣≤1 on [−1,1]. Since ∑i​γi​<∞, the Weierstrass M-test shows that
f(x)=∑i=1∞​γi​T3i​(x)
(9)
converges uniformly on [−1,1]. Every partial sum is continuous, so the uniform limit theorem makes f a well-defined continuous function.
Let
Pn​=∑i=1n​γi​T3i​,xk​=−cos3n+1kπ​(0≤k≤3n+1).
(10)
Then −1=x0​<x1​<⋯<x3n+1​=1. Since every 3i is odd and, for i≥n+1, 3i−n−1 is an odd integer,
T3i​(xk​)=−cos(kπ3i−n−1)=(−1)k+1.
(11)
It follows that
f(xk​)−Pn​(xk​)=(−1)k+1i=n+1∑∞​γi​​.
(12)
Thus the error has equal alternating extrema at 3n+1+1 ordered points. The Chebyshev alternation theorem shows that Pn​ is a best uniform approximation among polynomials of degree at most 3n+1−1, and in particular
E3n+1−1​(f):=infdegP≤3n+1−1​∥f−P∥∞​≥∑i=n+1∞​γi​.
(13)
Now let (δN​) be the prescribed decreasing positive sequence. Define
s0​=δ1​+1,sj​=δ3j​+2−j(j≥1),γj​=sj−1​−sj​.
(14)
Then sj​ decreases strictly to zero, so every γj​>0, the series ∑j​γj​=s0​ converges, and
∑i=j+1∞​γi​=sj​≥δ3j​.
(15)
Given N≥1, choose j≥0 with 3j≤N≤3j+1−1. Monotonicity of best-approximation errors and of δN​ gives
EN​(f)≥E3j+1−1​(f)≥sj​≥δ3j​≥δN​.
(16)
Hence this continuous f satisfies
t∈[−1,1]sup​∣f(t)−P(t)∣≥δN​​
(17)
for every polynomial P of degree at most N. This is the polynomial form of Bernstein's lethargy theorem.

Words: 129 Articles: 1

Solution

Words: 129
3G OurBigBook.com
For finite-valued discrete random variables, the conditional entropy is
H(X∣Y)=∑y​P(Y=y)H(X∣Y=y)=−∑x,y​p(x,y)log2​p(x∣y).
(18)
The chain rule for information entropy in two orders gives
H(X,Z∣Y)=H(X∣Y)+H(Z∣X,Y)=H(Z∣Y)+H(X∣Y,Z).
(19)
Therefore
H(X∣Y)=H(X∣Y,Z)+H(Z∣Y)−H(Z∣X,Y)≤H(X∣Y,Z)+H(Z),
(20)
using nonnegativity of conditional entropy and the fact that conditioning reduces entropy. This proves the required inequality.
For Fano's inequality, let X take values in an alphabet of size m, let X=g(Y) be any estimator, and put
E=1{X=X}​,pe​=P(E=1).
(21)
Because E is determined by (X,Y),
H(X∣Y)=H(E,X∣Y)=H(E∣Y)+H(X∣E,Y).
(22)
Now H(E∣Y)≤H(E)=h2​(pe​). If E=0, X is determined by Y; if E=1, at most m−1 values remain possible. Hence
H(X∣E,Y)≤pe​log2​(m−1).
(23)
Combining the bounds yields
H(X∣Y)≤h2​(pe​)+pe​log2​(m−1)​.
(24)

Solution

ii OurBigBook.com
This language is not context-free. Suppose it had pumping length N, and choose a prime p>N. Apply the pumping lemma to w=0p1p. Let α and β be the total numbers of zeros and ones in the pumped pieces v and y. If α=β, pumping with i=0 produces unequal block lengths and leaves the language. If α=β, then ∣vy∣>0 forces α=β=d>0. Pumping with i=p+1 produces equal block lengths
p+pd=p(1+d),
(28)
which are composite. Every possible pumping decomposition fails, proving the equal prime block language is not context-free.

Take context-free grammars GL​,GM​ for L,M and rename their nonterminals so that they are disjoint. If their start symbols are SL​,SM​, add a new start symbol S and the production
S→SL​SM​.
(32)
All productions remain context-free. A derivation from S produces a word from L followed by a word from M, and every such concatenation has a derivation. Thus the new grammar generates LM, proving closure of context-free languages under concatenation.

6C (Mathematical Biology)

Words: 182 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 182
6C OurBigBook.com
In this discrete age-structured population model, individuals of age a≥1 present during the breeding season each produce ba​ newborns, so the number entering age zero is
n0,t​=∑a=1∞​na,t​ba​.
(41)
An age-a individual survives the following winter with probability 1−μa​ and is then age a+1 in the next year, giving
na+1,t+1​=(1−μa​)na,t​.
(42)
Together with the initial age distribution, these equations determine every later cohort.
Substitute na,t​=ra​γt into the survival equation. Then
ra+1​=γ1−μa​​ra​,
(43)
and iteration gives
ra​=r0​γ−a∏i=0a−1​(1−μi​).
(44)
The birth equation becomes
r0​=∑a=1∞​ra​ba​=r0​∑a=1∞​[∏i=0a−1​(1−μi​)]γ−aba​.
(45)
A nonzero population mode therefore requires the Discrete Euler-Lotka equation
ϕ(γ)=1​,ϕ(γ)=∑a=1∞​[∏i=0a−1​(1−μi​)]γ−aba​.
(46)
For nonnegative vital rates with at least one surviving reproductive age and enough decay to make the series finite, ϕ is continuous and strictly decreasing on γ>0, tends to infinity as γ↓0, and tends to zero as γ→∞. The intermediate value theorem gives one positive solution, and strict monotonicity makes it unique.
The value ϕ(1) is the expected lifetime offspring count under these fixed rates. Since ϕ decreases, ϕ(1)>1 places the root at γ>1 and the population grows geometrically; ϕ(1)<1 places it at γ<1 and the population shrinks. Equality gives replacement, γ=1.

Let
ξi​(t)=∂s∂Qi​(s,t)​​s=0​
(54)
be the infinitesimal generator of the continuous symmetry, and let
pi​=∂q˙​i​∂L​
(55)
be the canonical momentum. Noether theorem states that along every trajectory satisfying the Euler-Lagrange equations,
J=i=1∑n​pi​ξi​​
(56)
is conserved.
Indeed, differentiate the invariance of L with respect to s at zero:
0=∑i​(∂qi​∂L​ξi​+∂q˙​i​∂L​ξ˙​i​).
(57)
On an Euler-Lagrange trajectory, ∂L/∂qi​=dpi​/dt, so
0=∑i​(p˙​i​ξi​+pi​ξ˙​i​)=dtd​∑i​pi​ξi​.
(58)
This proves the Noether conserved quantity for a mechanical point symmetry.

L=2m​(r˙2+r2ϕ˙​2+z˙2)−f(r,ϕ−kz).
(59)
The screw transformation
z↦z+s,ϕ↦ϕ+ks

For an infinitesimal test mass δm on the surface of a homogeneous sphere, its Newtonian mechanical energy is
E=21​δmR˙2−RGMδm​.
(62)
The spatially flat case corresponds to zero specific energy. Using
M=34π​ρR3
(63)
and dividing by δmR2/2 gives
(RR˙​)2=38πG​ρ.
(64)
Since R is proportional to the scale factor a, this is the Newtonian derivation of the flat Friedmann equation
H2=(aa˙​)2=38πG​ρ​.
(65)
Now take a(t0​)=1 and ρ=ρ0​a−4. Put
C=38πGρ0​​​.
(66)
The contracting branch of the Friedmann equation is
aa˙​=−Ca−2,a˙=−aC​.
(67)
Integrating ada=−Cdt from t0​ gives
21​(a(t)2−1)=−C(t−t0​).
(68)
Therefore
a(t)=1−2C(t−t0​)​​
(69)
on the contracting interval, reaching a=0 at t=t0​+1/(2C).

Write ∣α⟩=a∣0⟩+b∣1⟩. Expanding in the orthonormal Bell basis of systems CA gives the Bell-basis teleportation identity
∣α⟩C​∣β00​⟩AB​=21​(∣β00​⟩CA​∣α⟩B​+∣β01​⟩CA​Z∣α⟩B​+∣β10​⟩CA​X∣α⟩B​+∣β11​⟩CA​XZ∣α⟩B​).
(70)
Thus, uniformly for x,z∈{0,1},
∣μxz​⟩=XxZz∣α⟩​.
(71)
The states are unique because the four Bell states are an orthonormal basis of the two-qubit space. In particular,
∣μ10​⟩=X∣α⟩​.
(72)

b OurBigBook.com
Alice performs a projective Bell-basis measurement on her qubits C and A. Outcome (x,z) occurs with probability 1/4 and leaves Bob's qubit in
XxZz∣α⟩.
(73)
Alice sends the two classical bits (x,z) to Bob. He applies the inverse Pauli operation
(XxZz)−1=ZzXx,
(74)
recovering ∣α⟩ exactly, up to an irrelevant global phase. This is quantum teleportation: only local operations and classical communication are used, while the shared Bell pair supplies the entanglement resource.

Solution

c OurBigBook.com
No. Before any operation, Bob's reduced density matrix is I/2, independent of ∣α⟩. Any trace-preserving operation performed only by Alice leaves Bob's reduced state unchanged when her uncommunicated outcomes are averaged. This is the no-communication theorem, or quantum no-signalling.
If Bob received the unknown state, his reduced state would instead be the pure state ∣α⟩⟨α∣, which depends on Alice's input. That would let Alice signal by choosing different inputs, contradicting no-signalling. The two classical outcome bits are therefore essential.

kerπS​=⟨x⟩

has dimension one, and the punctured code C′=πS​(C) has length n−d and rank k−1 by the rank-nullity theorem.

wt(y′)+r≥d,wt(y′)+d−r≥d.

d′≥⌈2d​⌉​.

Let δ be the extended transition function of a deterministic finite automaton. States p,q∈Q are equivalent, or indistinguishable, when
p∼q⟺(δ(p,w)∈F⟺δ(q,w)∈F)for every w∈Σ∗.
(84)
The quotient deterministic finite automaton by indistinguishable states D/∼ has state set Q/∼, initial state [q0​], accepting states {[q]:q∈F}, and transition
δ([q],a)=[δ(q,a)].
(85)
Right invariance of ∼ makes this well-defined, and the quotient accepts L(D).
To prove minimality, choose for each state q of the accessible automaton D a word wq​ with δD​(q0​,wq​)=q. Run the same word in any DFA A accepting L(D), and assign the class [q] the reached state of A. If two distinct classes [p]=[q] reached the same state of A, every continuation u would have the same acceptance result after wp​ and wq​. Since A and D accept the same language, this would make p and q indistinguishable in D, a contradiction. Thus A has at least one distinct state for every class in D/∼, proving that the quotient is the minimal deterministic finite automaton.
For divisibility by seven, take states Q={0,1,…,6}, initial state 0, accepting set F={0}, and transitions
δ(r,b)=2r+b(mod7)​,b∈{0,1}.
(86)
After reading a word, the state is its binary value modulo seven, so this binary divisibility automaton accepts exactly the multiples of seven, with leading zeros allowed. Every state is accessible: the three-bit words representing 0,1,…,6 reach the corresponding residues.
For distinct residues p,q, let wp​ be the three-bit representation of −p(mod7), chosen in {0,…,6}. Since 23≡1(mod7), reading wp​ from state p ends at
23p+(−p)=0(mod7),
(87)
whereas reading it from q ends at q−p=0. Thus wp​ distinguishes p from q. All seven states are pairwise distinguishable, so the DFA is minimal by the Myhill-Nerode theorem.

Both variables are ordinal categorical variables, and the proposed alternative is directional: higher scores should tend to occur at higher prices. Assign increasing numerical scores to low, medium, high price and to poor, good, excellent quality, and use a one-sided linear-by-linear association test. Its statistic is based on the sample covariance, or equivalently the correlation, of those scores under the fixed margins.
This test uses one degree of freedom and directs its rejection region toward positive association. The four-degree-of-freedom likelihood-ratio test of independence in a contingency table spends power on every possible departure from independence, including unordered and negative patterns, so the ordered one-sided test is more powerful when the stated alternative is credible.

The Papperitz symbol
P⎩⎨⎧​aαα′​bββ′​cγγ′​;z⎭⎬⎫​
(99)
represents the two-dimensional solution space of a homogeneous linear differential equation for a second-order Fuchsian differential equation on the Riemann sphere. Its only singularities are the three regular singular points a,b,c. The two entries beneath each point are its characteristic exponents at a regular singular point: for example, in the nonresonant case a local basis near a has leading behaviours (z−a)α and (z−a)α′. If one of the points is infinity, exponent ρ conventionally means behaviour z−ρ there.
The six exponents obey the Fuchs relation
α+α′+β+β′+γ+γ′=1​.
(100)
Subject to this relation, the symbol determines the corresponding Riemann differential equation; resonant differences between exponents may produce Logarithmic Frobenius solutions without changing the exponent data recorded by the symbol.

In the decelerating hot Big Bang model, the particle horizon at recombination encloses only a finite comoving region. Widely separated parts of the cosmic microwave background therefore had no overlapping past light cones in that model, although they have almost the same temperature. This is the horizon problem. During cosmic inflation, accelerated expansion makes the comoving Hubble radius (aH)−1 shrink. A small region that was initially in causal contact can then expand to contain the whole presently observable universe.
The flatness problem follows from
∣Ω−1∣=a2H2∣k∣​.
(124)
During ordinary radiation- or matter-dominated decelerating expansion this quantity grows, so the observed closeness of the cosmological density parameter Ω to one requires extreme tuning at early times. Inflation makes aH grow nearly exponentially and therefore drives ∣Ω−1∣ rapidly toward zero. A sufficiently large number of e-folds makes spatial flatness a dynamical outcome rather than a finely tuned initial condition.

The completeness theorem for propositional logic states that for every set of formulae Γ and formula φ,
Γ⊨φ⟹Γ⊢φ​.
(125)
With the soundness theorem for propositional logic, this is an equivalence. It is also equivalent to saying that every consistent set of formulae has a model.
The usual countable proof lists all formulae and extends a consistent theory one formula at a time. For an uncountable set of primitive propositions, use the uncountable-language proof of propositional completeness: order the consistent extensions of Γ by inclusion. The union of every chain is consistent, since a proof of a contradiction would use only finitely many assumptions and hence would already lie in one member of the chain. Zorn lemma gives a maximal consistent set in propositional logic M. Define a Boolean valuation by v(p)=1 exactly when p∈M. The usual structural induction on formulae proves the truth lemma
v(θ)=1⟺θ∈M,
(126)
so v is a model of Γ.
The propositional compactness theorem says that a set Γ is satisfiable if and only if every finite subset of Γ is satisfiable. Only the forward implication is immediate. For the converse, if Γ had no model, then Γ⊨⊥, so completeness would give Γ⊢⊥. Every formal proof uses finitely many assumptions, so some finite Γ0​⊆Γ would prove ⊥ and, by soundness, would have no model, a contradiction.
The decidability theorem for propositional logic says that there is an algorithm deciding whether a propositional formula is a theorem. A formula contains only finitely many primitive propositions, even when the full language is uncountable. Its finite truth table decides whether it is valid, and completeness says that validity is equivalent to theoremhood.
Now let (X,<) be the given partially ordered set. For every distinct x,y∈X, introduce propositions pxy​ and qxy​. Form a propositional theory T containing the following clauses:
  • pxy​↔¬pyx​ and qxy​↔¬qyx​ for distinct x,y;
  • (pxy​∧pyz​)→pxz​ and (qxy​∧qyz​)→qxz​ for pairwise distinct x,y,z;
  • pxy​ and qxy​ whenever x<y in the original order;
  • ¬(pxy​∧qxy​) and ¬(pyx​∧qyx​) whenever x and y are incomparable in the original order.
The first two families say that p and q encode strict total orders. The third makes both orders extend <, while the fourth makes them disagree on every incomparable pair.
Every finite subset T0​⊆T mentions only a finite subset F⊆X. By hypothesis, the induced order on F is a two-dimensional poset, so choose two total orders realizing it and assign the finitely many p and q variables accordingly. This satisfies T0​. Thus every finite subset of T is satisfiable, and propositional compactness gives a model of all of T.
Define x<1​y when pxy​ is true and x<2​y when qxy​ is true. The clauses make <1​ and <2​ total orders on X. They both contain the original order, and their intersection contains no incomparable pair. Hence
x<y⟺x<1​y and x<2​y,
(127)
which proves the finite-local characterization of two-dimensional partially ordered sets.

Ae=de​,

If Av=dv, then the quadratic form of the Graph Laplacian L=dI−A gives

Every summand is nonnegative, so vi​=vj​ along every edge. The graph is connected, hence all coordinates of v are equal and v is a scalar multiple of e. Thus the d-eigenspace is one-dimensional. Since A is a symmetric matrix, the spectral theorem for real symmetric matrices makes it diagonalizable, so the algebraic multiplicity is also one. This proves the constant eigenvector of a regular graph result.

Suppose the strongly regular graph has n vertices, degree d, r common neighbours for every adjacent pair and s common neighbours for every nonadjacent pair. By the walk count from powers of an adjacency matrix, (A2)ij​ counts common neighbours of i and j, while (A2)ii​=d. Hence the adjacency-matrix relation for a strongly regular graph is
A2=(d−s)I+(r−s)A+sJ,

where J is the all-ones matrix.
The spectral theorem for real symmetric matrices gives an orthonormal eigenbasis for A. Part (a) says that the constant direction is the one-dimensional d-eigenspace; every other eigenvector v belongs to e⊥, so Jv=0. If Av=θv, the displayed identity gives
θ2−(r−s)θ−(d−s)=0.

There are at most two possible roots θ in addition to d. Thus G has at most three distinct eigenvalues.

Solution

Words: 94
a OurBigBook.com
Schur lemma over C states that an intertwining operator T:V→W between finite-dimensional irreducible complex representations is either zero or an isomorphism. In particular, every intertwining endomorphism of V is a scalar multiple of the identity.
Indeed, kerT⊆V and imT⊆W are invariant subspaces. If T=0, irreducibility gives kerT=0 and imT=W, so T is an isomorphism. For an endomorphism T:V→V, the fundamental theorem of algebra gives an eigenvalue λ∈C. Then T−λI is an intertwiner with nonzero kernel, so the first part forces T−λI=0. Hence T=λI, completing the Proof of Schur lemma.

c0​=∑j=0n−1​ej​

For each 1≤k<n/2, define the real discrete Fourier modes

The plane Wk​=span{ck​,sk​} is invariant, and g acts on it by rotation through 2πk/n. Since this angle is neither zero nor π, Wk​ is irreducible over R. The traces 2cos(2πk/n) are distinct for 1≤k<n/2, so these modules are pairwise nonisomorphic. Orthogonality of the discrete Fourier transform gives
RCn​=⟨c0​⟩⊕⟨cn/2​⟩⊕k=1⨁(n−2)/2​Wk​​.

The dimensions sum to 1+1+2(n−2)/2=n, so this is the whole regular module: two nonisomorphic one-dimensional summands and (n−2)/2 nonisomorphic two-dimensional summands.

p∘f​1​=f=p∘f​2​

and f​1​(y0​)=f​2​(y0​) at one point y0​∈Y, then

Take X=S1∨S1, the wedge of two circles, and label its oriented loops a and b. For a fixed n≥3, let
α=(1 2 ⋯ n),β=(1 2)
(179)
be permutations of the fibre {1,…,n}. Construct a labelled graph Xn​ with these n vertices, an oriented a-edge from i to α(i), and an oriented b-edge from i to β(i). Map every vertex to the wedge point and each labelled edge homeomorphically onto its corresponding loop. Every vertex has exactly one incoming and one outgoing edge of each label, so this is an n-sheeted permutation covering of a wedge of circles
pn​:Xn​⟶X.
(180)
It is connected because the n-cycle α acts transitively on the fibre.
A deck transformation induces a permutation γ of the vertices that commutes with both monodromy permutations α and β. Conversely, such a permutation determines a deck transformation, by the deck transformation group as a monodromy centralizer. The permutations α and β generate Sn​: the conjugates αjβα−j include the adjacent transpositions, which generate the symmetric group. Hence γ centralizes Sn​ and lies in its center of a group. For n≥3, the center of Sn​ is trivial, so γ=1. A deck transformation fixing one point is the identity by part (a), and therefore
Deck(pn​)={1}​.
(181)

No. The monodromy action of a covering space for a two-sheeted covering takes values in S2​. Its nonidentity transposition commutes with every subgroup of S2​, so the deck transformation group as a monodromy centralizer always contains that transposition. Equivalently, every double cover has a deck involution of a double covering that exchanges the two points in each fibre. Thus a two-sheeted cover cannot have trivial deck group.

A continuous-time Markov chain is irreducible if every state can reach every other state with positive probability. A state i is recurrent if, after leaving i, the chain returns to i with probability one; an irreducible chain is recurrent if one, and hence every, state is recurrent. A recurrent state is positive recurrent if its expected continuous first return time is finite, and an irreducible chain is positive recurrent when all its states are.

Li​∣j⟩=−iℏεikj​∣k⟩,L2∣j⟩=2ℏ2∣j⟩.
(329)
Since the orbital angular momentum eigenvalue is ℓ(ℓ+1)ℏ2, every first-excited state has
ℓ=1.​
(330)
Finally,
Lz​∣x⟩=iℏ∣y⟩,Lz​∣y⟩=−iℏ∣x⟩.
(331)
Therefore the normalized magnetic quantum number m=+1 state can be chosen as
∣ψ⟩=2​∣x⟩+i∣y⟩​=2​Ax†​+iAy†​​∣0⟩,​
(332)
which obeys Lz​∣ψ⟩=ℏ∣ψ⟩ and ∥∣ψ⟩∥=1.

Choose the Landau gauge
A=(0,Bx,0),ϕ=0.
(333)
It preserves translation invariance in the y-direction, so py​=ℏk is conserved. With pz​=0, magnetic minimal coupling gives
H=2m1​[px2​+(py​−qBx)2]=2mpx2​​+2mωc2​​(x−xk​)2,
(334)
where
ωc​=m∣qB∣​,xk​=qBℏk​.
(335)
This is a quantum harmonic oscillator, so the Landau levels are
En​=ℏωc​(n+21​),n=0,1,2,…,​
(336)
independent of k.
The periodic boundary condition in y quantizes k=2πr/Ly​. Requiring the guiding centre to lie in a strip of width Lx​ gives a k-interval of width ∣qB∣Lx​/ℏ. The number of allowed integers is therefore approximately
D=2πLy​​ℏ∣qB∣Lx​​=2πℏ∣qB∣A​,​
(337)
the degeneracy of a Landau level, up to boundary corrections.

Keep A=(0,Bx,0) and choose the scalar potential ϕ=−Ex. Then
H=2m1​[px2​+(py​−qBx)2+pz2​]−qEx.
(338)
For pz​=0, completing the square gives
H=2mpx2​​+2mωc2​​(x−xc​)2−BE​py​−2B2mE2​,xc​=qBpy​​+qB2mE​.
(339)
Hence the spectrum on R3 is
En​(k)=ℏωc​(n+21​)−BE​ℏk−2B2mE2​.​
(340)
For a translationally invariant dispersion, the group velocity is vy​=ℏ−1∂En​/∂k. Therefore
vy​=−BE​,​
(341)
in agreement with the electric-cross-magnetic-field drift E×B/B2.
In the rectangle, k=2πr/Ly​ as before. The energy now changes with r, so the guiding-centre degeneracy is lifted, while the number of states in each tilted band remains approximately ∣qB∣A/(2πℏ). Adjacent states within a formerly degenerate level have the electric-field splitting of a Landau level in a rectangle
ΔEelectric​=Ly​2πℏ​​BE​​.​
(342)
Thus this is the ground-to-first-excited gap when the lowest Landau band contains at least two allowed guiding centres and ΔEelectric​<ℏωc​. Without that implicit weak-field or large-sample condition, the exact full spectral gap is
ΔE=min{∣B∣Ly​2πℏ∣E∣​,ℏωc​}.​
(343)

35D (Statistical Physics)

Words: 239 Articles: 4
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

a

Words: 161 Articles: 1
35D OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 161
a OurBigBook.com
Macroscopically, an adiabatic process exchanges no heat with its surroundings: δQ=0. A reversible adiabatic process is therefore isentropic, since dS=δQrev​/T=0. Microscopically, the system is thermally isolated, so changes in its energy arise from work done by changing external parameters rather than random energy exchange with a heat bath; in a sufficiently slow change, the populations of the corresponding microscopic states are carried along without producing entropy.
For repeated operation the working substance must execute a thermodynamic cycle. Reversible isothermal contact at T2​ absorbs heat Q2​, a reversible adiabat changes the temperature to T1​, reversible isothermal contact at T1​ rejects heat Q1​>0, and a second adiabat returns to the initial state. This is the Carnot cycle. Reversibility and zero net entropy change give
T2​Q2​​−T1​Q1​​=0,Q2​Q1​​=T2​T1​​.
(344)
The thermal efficiency is the net work output divided by the absorbed heat:
η=Q2​W​=Q2​Q2​−Q1​​.
(345)
Consequently
ηmax​=1−T2​T1​​.​
(346)
The Carnot theorem shows that any irreversible cycle has smaller efficiency, so the two isotherms joined by two adiabats are optimal.

b

Words: 78 Articles: 1
35D OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 78
b OurBigBook.com
At fixed volume, entropy from heat capacity obeys dS=C(T)dT/T. The Third law of thermodynamics fixes S(0)=0 when the ground state is nondegenerate, so below the transition
S(Tc−​)=∫0Tc​​TαT​dT=αTc​.
(347)
Above the transition,
S(T)=S(Tc+​)+∫Tc​T​T′β​dT′=S(Tc+​)+βlogTc​T​.
(348)
For a transition with no latent heat, entropy is continuous, and comparison with S=βlogT+γ gives the directly testable relation
γ=αTc​−βlogTc​.​
(349)
Thus calorimetric measurements of C(T) and Tc​ verify γ. More generally, if a measurable latent heat L is present, S(Tc+​)−S(Tc−​)=L/Tc​, and the formula becomes
γ=αTc​+Tc​L​−βlogTc​.​
(350)

For a constant electromagnetic field tensor, the relativistic Lorentz force is a linear system with constant coefficients, so
uμ(τ)=[exp(mq​Fτ)]μν​uν(0).​
(351)
Put
a=mcqE​,b=mqB​,γ0​=1−v02​/c2​1​.
(352)
The initial four-velocity is (u0,u1,u2,u3)=γ0​(c,0,v0​,0). For parallel fields along x, the field tensor has one hyperbolic block in the (0,1) plane and one rotation block in the (2,3) plane. With the orientation convention in the question,
u0=γ0​ccosh(aτ),u1=γ0​csinh(aτ),
(353)
u2=γ0​v0​cos(bτ),u3=−γ0​v0​sin(bτ).
(354)
Taking the initial spacetime point to be the origin and integrating uμ=dxμ/dτ gives the relativistic motion in parallel electric and magnetic fields
t(τ)x(τ)y(τ)z(τ)​=aγ0​​sinh(aτ),=aγ0​c​(cosh(aτ)−1),=bγ0​v0​​sin(bτ),=bγ0​v0​​(cos(bτ)−1).​​
(355)
The expressions have their continuous a→0 or b→0 limits when one field vanishes; reversing the sign of q reverses the electric acceleration and magnetic rotation.
Eliminating proper time between the first two equations yields
x(t)=aγ0​c​​1+(γ0​at​)2​−1​.​
(356)
At early coordinate time,
x(t)=2mγ0​qE​t2+O(t4),
(357)
which is uniformly accelerated motion with the transverse relativistic inertia factor γ0​. At late positive time,
x(t)=sgn(qE)ct−qEγ0​mc2​+O(t−1),
(358)
so the longitudinal speed approaches the speed of light.
The y-z projection satisfies
y2+(z+bγ0​v0​​)2=(bγ0​v0​​)2.
(359)
It is therefore a circle of radius and proper-time period
R=∣q∣Bγ0​m∣v0​∣​,Δτ=∣q∣B2πm​.​
(360)
For the pitch magnitude assume v0​>0 and put α=∣q∣E/(mc), Ω=∣q∣B/m, and
r=αΔτ=cB2πE​.
(361)
Number the nth proper-time period as [(n−1)Δτ,nΔτ]. Its longitudinal displacement is
Δxn​=αγ0​c​[cosh(nr)−cosh((n−1)r)].
(362)
Consequently, as n→∞,
Pn​=RΔxn​​∼2αv0​cΩ​(1−e−r)enr=Aexp(cB2πEn​),
(363)
where
A=2Ev0​c2B​(1−e−2πE/(cB)).​
(364)

Because the Levi-Civita connection is torsion-free, its Christoffel symbols satisfy Γραμ​=Γαρμ​. Substitute the stated coordinate expression for each term in the cyclic sum
Rμραβ​+Rμβρα​+Rμαβρ​.
(365)
The partial-derivative terms cancel pairwise by the lower-index symmetry of Γ, and the quadratic terms cancel after relabelling their dummy indices. Therefore
Rμραβ​+Rμβρα​+Rμαβρ​=0,​
(366)
which is the first Bianchi identity.

Expanding the two covariant derivatives of a vector, the second partial derivatives cancel in the commutator. The remaining derivatives and products of Christoffel symbols combine into the coordinate definition of the Riemann curvature tensor, giving the Ricci identity
2∇[α​∇β]​Vγ=[∇α​,∇β​]Vγ=Rγραβ​Vρ.​
(367)
For a type-(2,0) tensor, the connection acts on both upper indices, so the curvature commutator on a contravariant tensor is
2∇[α​∇β]​Tμν=Rμραβ​Tρν+Rνραβ​Tμρ.​
(368)

∇ν​∇μ​Kα​=21​([∇ν​,∇μ​]Kα​−[∇μ​,∇α​]Kν​+[∇α​,∇ν​]Kμ​).
(369)

The Killing equation gives ∇μ​Kμ=0 and ∇[μ​Kλ]​=∇μ​Kλ​. Commuting derivatives once and contracting the Ricci identity gives
∇λ∇μ​Kλ​=Rμβ​Kβ.
(373)
Therefore, using the contracted Bianchi identity and symmetry of Rμβ​,
2∇μ∇λ∇[μ​Kλ]​​=2∇μ(Rμβ​Kβ)=Kβ∇β​R+2Rμβ​∇μKβ=Kβ∇β​R.​
(374)
Since ∇[μ​Kλ]​ is antisymmetric, swapping the two contracted index names shows that the left side equals its derivative-antisymmetrized form:
Kα∇α​R=2∇[μ∇λ]∇[μ​Kλ]​.​

Now set Aμλ​=∇[μ​Kλ]​. The right side is the contracted commutator [∇μ,∇λ]Aμλ​. By the curvature commutator on a covariant tensor, it is a sum of contractions of the symmetric Ricci tensor with the antisymmetric tensor A, and hence vanishes. Thus
Kα∇α​R=0,​

Let u(r,z) and w(r,z) be the radial and vertical velocity components. For steady incompressible axisymmetric flow without swirl, mass conservation and the relevant cylindrical components of the Navier-Stokes equation are
r1​∂r∂(ru)​+∂z∂w​=0,
(377)
ρ(u∂r∂u​+w∂z∂u​)=−∂r∂p​+μ(∂r2∂2u​+r1​∂r∂u​−r2u​+∂z2∂2u​),
(378)
ρ(u∂r∂w​+w∂z∂w​)=−∂z∂p​+μ(∂r2∂2w​+r1​∂r∂w​+∂z2∂2w​).
(379)
The vertical scale is w∼V. Incompressibility over radial scale R and gap scale h gives u∼VR/h=V/ε. In the radial equation, inertia is smaller than transverse viscous stress by
μρVh​=Re≪1,
(380)
while radial viscous derivatives are smaller than uzz​ by ε2. The pressure scale is μVR2/h3. In the vertical equation, both viscous and inertial terms are smaller than the corresponding cross-gap pressure-gradient scale by at least O(ε2). Thus the leading lubrication theory equations are
r1​(ru)r​+wz​=0,pr​=μuzz​,pz​=0.​
(381)

Away from the rim's O(h) edge region, the geometry and uniform injection have no radial scale other than the factor required by continuity. It is therefore consistent to take w=w(z). Regularity at r=0 then lets the continuity equation integrate to
u(r,z)=−2r​w′(z).
(382)
The no-slip boundary condition and prescribed normal velocities are
w(0)=V,w′(0)=0,w(h)=0,w′(h)=0.
(383)
Since p is independent of z, the radial equation implies that w′′′ is constant. The four boundary conditions give
w(z)=V[1−3(hz​)2+2(hz​)3],
(384)
and hence
u(r,z)=h3Vr​hz​(1−hz​).
(385)
Using w′′′=12V/h3 in pr​=μuzz​ gives
pr​=−h36μVr​.
(386)
Taking the pressure at the rim to be atmospheric, p(R)=p0​, produces the porous-plate lubrication cushion pressure
p(r)−p0​=h33μV​(R2−r2).​
(387)
The upward pressure force balances the disc's weight:
W=∫0R​[p(r)−p0​],2πrdr=2h33πμVR4​.
(388)
Since ε=h/R,
W=2ε33πμVR​.​
(389)

The one-dimensional Isentropic Euler equations are
ρt​+uρx​+ρux​=0,ut​+uux​+ρ1​px​=0.
(390)
For the polytropic equation of state,
c2=dρdp​=ργp​,c0​c​=(ρ0​ρ​)(γ−1)/2.
(391)
The continuity equation therefore implies
ct​+ucx​+2γ−1​cux​=0,
(392)

ut​+uux​+γ−12c​cx​=0.
(393)

[∂t​+(u±c)∂x​][u±γ−12(c−c0​)​]=0.
(394)

R±​=u±γ−12(c−c0​)​​

C±​:dtdx​=u±c.​

The undisturbed gas has u=0, c=c0​, and hence R−​=0. The disturbance from the receding piston is a right-moving simple wave, so this invariant remains zero throughout it:
c=c0​+2γ−1​u,ρ=ρ0​(1+2c0​γ−1​u)2/(γ−1).
(397)
Let s be the time at which the relevant C+​ characteristic leaves the piston. The boundary condition is u=X˙p​(s) there. Both u and c are constant along this characteristic, whose speed is
u+c=c0​+2γ+1​X˙p​(s).
(398)
Hence s=s(x,t) is determined implicitly by the receding-piston rarefaction wave equation
x=Xp​(s)+[c0​+2γ+1​X˙p​(s)](t−s).​
(399)
Within Xp​(t)<x<c0​t, the solution is therefore
u(x,t)=X˙p​(s(x,t)),​
(400)
ρ(x,t)=ρ0​[1+2c0​γ−1​X˙p​(s(x,t))]2/(γ−1).​
(401)
For x≥c0​t, the gas remains undisturbed: u=0 and ρ=ρ0​. The speed bound keeps c and ρ positive, and monotonic increase of ∣X˙p​∣ makes this an expanding rarefaction wave rather than a characteristic-crossing compression.

xv​(t)=Xp​(tc​)−γ−12c0​​(t−tc​).​

Choose a matrix splitting A=M−N with M invertible. Then Ax=b is equivalent to
x=M−1Nx+M−1b,
(409)
and the associated stationary iterative method for a linear system is
x(k+1)=Hx(k)+M−1b,H=M−1N.
(410)
For the Jacobi method, write A=D+L+U with D diagonal and L,U strictly lower and upper triangular, and take
M=D,N=−(L+U).
(411)
Thus
x(k+1)=−D−1(L+U)x(k)+D−1b.​
(412)
The iteration converges for every initial vector exactly when the spectral radius of its iteration matrix satisfies
ρ(−D−1(L+U))<1.​
(413)

b OurBigBook.com
Here D=I, so the Jacobi iteration matrix is
H=I−A=​0−α−α​−α0−α​−α−α0​​.
(414)
The all-ones vector is an eigenvector with eigenvalue −2α. On its two-dimensional orthogonal complement, the coordinates sum to zero and Hv=αv, so the other eigenvalue is α with multiplicity two. Therefore
ρ(H)=max{2∣α∣,∣α∣}=2∣α∣.
(415)
By Jacobi convergence for a three-by-three equicorrelation matrix, convergence occurs exactly for
−21​<α<21​.​
(416)
At either endpoint the spectral radius is one, so convergence for arbitrary initial data fails.

Solution

c OurBigBook.com
The Householder-John theorem states: if A=M−N is Hermitian positive definite and M∗+N is also Hermitian positive definite, then M is invertible and
ρ(M−1N)<1.
(417)
Now let A=D+L+LT be real symmetric positive definite and tridiagonal. For the Jacobi splitting, M=D and N=−(L+LT). Positive definiteness of A implies every diagonal entry is positive, so D is positive definite. Introduce the alternating-sign diagonal matrix
S=diag(1,−1,1,−1,…).
(418)
Tridiagonality gives
SAS=D−L−LT=M∗+N.
(419)
Since S is orthogonal, SAS is positive definite whenever A is. Both hypotheses of the Householder-John theorem hold, and hence the Jacobi iteration matrix satisfies ρ(M−1N)<1. Therefore the Jacobi convergence for a symmetric positive-definite tridiagonal matrix follows.
